pages.name: Forwards and backwards
pages.text: [[Integrating]] is differentiating run backwards: you are given a rate and asked for the rule it came from. You know the forward direction already. The power rule takes `x³` to `3x²`: bring the 3 to the front, then take one off the power. So the question ‘whose derivative is `3x²`?’ has the answer `x³`. Wherever P goes on the curve `y = x³`, its tangent’s slope is `3x²`. Drag P.

pages.name: Whose derivative is 2x?
pages.task: Which rule has the derivative `2x`? At `x` = 1 its tangent must have slope 2 × 1 = 2.
pages.why: Run the power rule forwards on each answer. `x²` gives `2x`, so it is the one. `2x²` gives `2 × 2x = 4x`, twice too steep, and a plain 2 gives 0. The 2 is what you get by differentiating `2x`, the wrong way round.

pages.name: Add one, then divide
pages.text: To work backwards without guessing, undo the power rule’s two steps in the opposite order. Forwards, you bring the power to the front, then take one off it. Backwards, you add one to the power, then divide by the new power. For `x²`, add one to get `x³`, then divide by 3 to get `x³ ÷ 3`. Check it by differentiating: `3x² ÷ 3 = x²`, what you started with. On the curve, the tangent’s slope at P is P’s `x` squared.

pages.task: Which rule has the derivative `x³`? At `x` = 1 its tangent must have slope 1³ = 1.
pages.why: Add one to the power, 3 to 4, then divide by the new power: `x⁴ ÷ 4`. Check: `4x³ ÷ 4 = x³`. Dividing by the old power gives `x⁴ ÷ 3`, which differentiates to `4x³ ÷ 3`, a third too steep. `3x²` lowers the power: that is `x³` differentiated, not its reverse.

pages.name: Term by term
pages.text: A number in front carries through, and a sum is done one term at a time, because differentiating works that way forwards. So the example rate `6x² + 4x + 5` becomes `2x³ + 2x² + 5x`. The plain 5 comes from `5x`, whose slope is 5 everywhere. One power will not go: −1, which is `1 ÷ x`, because a power below zero means ‘one over’ (lesson 9 comes back to that). Adding one gives a power of 0, and you cannot divide by 0.

pages.name: Integrate 4x³ − 6x + 2
pages.task: Integrate the example rate `4x³ − 6x + 2`. At `x` = 1 it is 4 − 6 + 2 = 0, so the answer’s tangent there must be level.
pages.why: Term by term: `4x³` becomes 4 × `x⁴` ÷ 4 = `x⁴`, `−6x` becomes −6 × `x²` ÷ 2 = `−3x²`, and 2 becomes `2x`. Differentiate `x⁴ − 3x² + 2x` and `4x³ − 6x + 2` comes back. `12x² − 6` lowers the powers: that is differentiating. `4x⁴ − 6x² + 2x` raises them but never divides.

Above, the rule x to the fourth minus 3x squared plus 2x and its derivative 4x cubed minus 6x plus 2. 4x cubed becomes x to the fourth, minus 6x becomes minus 3x squared, 2 becomes 2x. Slope 4 minus 6 plus 2 equals 0 at x equals 1. Level there: it fits

pages.name: A family of curves
pages.text: Differentiating loses something. A plain number does not change as `x` changes, so its derivative is zero, and `x² + 5`, `x²` and `x² − 3` all differentiate to `2x`. Adding a number `c` lifts every point of the curve by the same amount. Both ends of any chord are lifted by `c`, so its rise and its slope are unchanged, however short it is, and the whole curve slides up or down without its steepness changing anywhere. The tangent at `x` = 2 keeps its slope, 4, while its height, `4 + c`, changes. Slide `c` and watch.
pages.alt: The family y equals x squared plus c. Above, the rule x squared plus c and its derivative 2x. Tangent at x equals 2: slope 2 times 2 equals 4. Its height: 4 plus c equals 4 plus 5 equals 9

pages.name: The whole family
pages.task: `x³` and `x³ + 4` have the same slope at every `x`: at `x` = 1 both have 3 × 1² = 3. What is the full answer to ‘whose derivative is `3x²`?’
pages.why: A plain number differentiates to 0, so `x³`, `x³ + 4` and `x³` plus any other number all differentiate to `3x²`. Working back cannot tell which one you came from, so the full answer is the whole family, `x³ + c`. That `c` is the [[constant of integration]], and it is easy to lose: on one 2023 Advanced Higher question, Scottish examiners reported many candidates making basic errors in applying a formula approach, or in dealing with the constant of integration.
pages.alt: y equals x cubed and y equals x cubed plus 4. Above, the rule x cubed plus c and its derivative 3x squared. A plain number differentiates to 0. So every x cubed plus c has slope 3x squared. The full answer: x cubed plus c

pages.name: One known value
pages.text: To pick one curve out of the family, you need one value you know. Say a capacitor charges with a current that rises steadily, `t` amps after `t` seconds. Current is the rate charge flows, so the charge is the current integrated, its [[integral]], written `∫ t dt` (∫ says integrate; `dt` says `t` is the letter that changes). Add one to the power, then divide by the new power: `t` becomes `t² ÷ 2 = 0.5t²`, so `q = 0.5t² + c` coulombs. Say it held 3 C at 0 s. Put `t` = 0 in: `0.5 × 0 + c = 3`, so `c` = 3, and at 4 s it holds `8 + 3 = 11` C. Leave `c` out and it starts at 0 C, 3 C short all the way along.

pages.name: A boat from 10 m out
pages.task: A boat’s speed is `2t` metres per second after `t` seconds, and it starts 10 m out from the quay, an example. Integrating, its distance from the quay is `s = t² + c` metres. How far out is it at 3 s?
pages.why: Integrate the speed: `2t` becomes `2 × t² ÷ 2 = t²`, plus `c`. At the start, `0 + c = 10`, so `c` = 10 and `s = t² + 10`. At 3 s that is `9 + 10 = 19` m. Without `c` the boat would start at 0 m, and 9 m is where that curve is at 3 s. Putting 3 into `2t` gives the speed then, 6 m/s, not a distance.

pages.name: Through 5 at x = 1
pages.task: An example rate, `6x² − 4x`, and `y` = 5 at `x` = 1. Which rule is it?
pages.why: Term by term: `6x²` becomes 6 × `x³` ÷ 3 = `2x³`, and `−4x` becomes −4 × `x²` ÷ 2 = `−2x²`, plus `c`. At `x` = 1, `2 − 2 + c = 5`, so `c` = 5. `6x³ − 4x² + 3` passes through the point but was never divided, so its slope there is 10, not 2. `2x³ − 2x²` has the right slopes but misses the point.

pages.name: Charge at 2 s
pages.task: A capacitor’s current is `3t²` amps after `t` seconds, and it holds 2 C at 1 s, an example. How much does it hold at 2 s?
pages.why: Integrate the current: `3t²` becomes `3 × t³ ÷ 3 = t³`, plus `c`. The value you know is at 1 s, not at the start, so put `t` = 1 in: `1 + c = 2`, so `c` = 1 and `q = t³ + 1`. At 2 s that is `8 + 1 = 9` C. Taking the 2 C as `c` gives a curve that holds 3 C at 1 s; leaving `c` out gives one that holds 1 C.
